title: James Crow on Glenn's Creek
summary: Scottish-born chemist and physician James Crow is credited with perfecting the sour mash process at the Pepper family distillery on Glenn's Creek.
bodyMarkdown:
James C. Crow was born about 1789 in Inverness, Scotland, and studied at Edinburgh University before coming to Kentucky around 1820. According to [a biography of James C. Crow](https://grokipedia.com/page/james_c._crow), he was a chemist and physician. He is credited with using and perfecting the sour mash process, and the Old Crow brand still carries his name.

## From Grier's Creek to Glenn's Creek

Crow's first Kentucky job was at Willis Field's distillery on Grier's Creek in Woodford County. His most important work came a few miles away, on Glenn's Creek, at the farm distillery of the Pepper family. [Grokipedia's article on Woodford Reserve](https://grokipedia.com/page/Woodford_Reserve) says Elijah Pepper began distilling in the area in 1812.

Crow was advising Oscar Pepper as early as 1833. From 1837 to 1838 Pepper built a new stone distillery, with stonework by the mason Thomas Mayhall. A drought from 1838 to 1840 interrupted production, and Crow returned for the 1840 season. He worked at the Pepper distillery until 1855 and was paid one-eighth of what he produced.

## Science and labor

Crow brought a scientist's habits to the stillhouse. He owned a hydrometer and a saccharometer, was said to have one of the largest personal libraries in Kentucky, and pursued chemistry as a hobby. In sour mash, part of an earlier batch is used to start the next. One account credits Crow with using and perfecting the method.

Another, Grokipedia's Woodford Reserve article, goes further and says he "introduced" it.

Crow did not work alone. He was assisted by two enslaved men, Dick and Albert, and by William F. Mitchell.

## A name on the barrel

In the 1840s Crow chalked the letters C-R-O-W on his barrel heads to mark them as his own. His whiskey was shipped beyond Kentucky to Canada, Europe and South America. After leaving Pepper, he divided his time among other distilleries. He died on April 20, 1856, after a stroke or heart attack in the Anderson Johnson stillhouse on Glenn's Creek, and his family was left nearly penniless.

The name outlived the man. Gaines, Berry & Co., formed in 1866, registered the Old Crow trademark in 1870. Old Crow is now produced by Suntory Global Spirits.

## Kentucky today

The old Pepper distillery on Glenn's Creek is now the Woodford Reserve Distillery, near [Versailles](/stories/versailles-takes-shape/). Grokipedia says the site is a National Historic Landmark and that Brown-Forman launched the Woodford Reserve brand in 1996. For a later chapter in bourbon's regulation, see [E. H. Taylor Jr. and the Bottled-in-Bond Act](/stories/e-h-taylor-jr-and-the-bottled-in-bond-act-1897/).
